analysis: The inverted cosmos of Canto 28, in which God is a point and the universe is wrapped around it, is one of the poem's boldest images, and some mathematicians and historians of science have compared its geometry to that of a hypersphere. It shows how Dante's cosmology is at once Aristotelian and visionary [[boyde1981]].

Beatrice's farewell speech in Canto 30 has surprised readers: the guide who has led Dante through the heavens ends with a promise of Henry VII's throne and the damnation of a pope. It is a sign of how far the poem's vision of eternity remains bound to the history of Dante's own time [[ferrante1984]] [[took2020]].

key.quote:
Light intellectual replete with love,
Love of true good replete with ecstasy,
Ecstasy that transcendeth every sweetness.
key.note: 'Luce intellettüal, piena d'amore': Beatrice defines the Empyrean as light that is both understanding and love.

books.title: Paradiso 31–33: The rose; Bernard; the vision of God
summary: The blessed are arranged in the white rose, and angels fly like bees between them and God. Dante turns to speak to Beatrice and finds instead an old man: St Bernard of Clairvaux, the great contemplative and devotee of the Virgin, who will guide him to the end. Beatrice has returned to her seat in the rose, and Dante thanks her in a prayer for leading him from slavery to freedom; she smiles and turns to the eternal fountain. In Canto 32 Bernard explains the order of the rose: the saints of the Old and New Testaments, separated by a line of women including Mary and Eve, and the souls of children saved before they could choose.

Canto 33 begins with Bernard's prayer to the Virgin: 'Virgin Mother, daughter of thy Son'. Mary looks favourably on Dante, and Bernard signals him to look up. Dante's sight passes into the eternal light, and he sees the universe bound by love into one volume, then three circles of three colours and one size, and in the second circle a human image. Like a geometer who tries to square the circle, he struggles to understand how the image fits the circle, until a flash of light fulfils his desire. His fantasy fails, but his desire and will are turned like a wheel by the love that moves the sun and the other stars.
analysis: The last canto is often ranked among the highest achievements of European poetry; T. S. Eliot judged it so in his essay of 1929 [[eliot1929]]. It achieves its effect less by description than by repeated admission of failure: memory fails, speech fails, the poet becomes a child at the breast. The final vision of the Incarnation is described through the image of the geometer, so that understanding comes not through argument but as a gift [[barolini1992]] [[jacoff2007]].

Bernard's replacement of Beatrice is the last of the poem's changes of guide. The poet's love for Beatrice is completed and surpassed by the contemplative's love for Mary. The final line gathers the whole poem into one image: the movement of desire, first lost in the dark wood, is at last moved in harmony with the love that moves the universe [[singleton1958]] [[freccero1986]].

key.quote:
Here vigour failed the lofty fantasy:
But now was turning my desire and will,
Even as a wheel that equally is moved,
key.note: Fantasy fails and the will turns like a wheel; the last line, 'l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle', names what moves it.

characters.name: Dante
characters.text: The pilgrim and the poet are the same man at different times: the pilgrim is the Dante of 1300, lost, frightened, curious and often wrong; the poet is the exile who writes years later and knows how the journey ended. Much of the poem's subtlety comes from the distance between them, which John Freccero described as the distance of conversion [[freccero1986]].

characters.name: Virgil
characters.text: The Roman poet of the Aeneid (70–19 BC), sent by Beatrice to guide Dante through Hell and Purgatory. He stands for the best of human reason and of classical poetry, and he is a loving, sometimes fallible father to Dante. Because he lived before Christ and did not believe, he belongs to Limbo, and he disappears at the top of the mountain when Beatrice arrives.

characters.name: Beatrice
characters.text: The Florentine woman Dante loved, who died in 1290 and whose story he told in the Vita Nuova. In the poem she sets the journey in motion, appears in the Earthly Paradise, reproaches Dante for his infidelity and leads him through the heavens. She is a real woman remembered and a figure of grace and revelation, and the relation between these roles is one of the poem's main questions.

characters.name: St Bernard of Clairvaux
characters.text: The twelfth-century Cistercian abbot and contemplative, famous for his devotion to the Virgin, who replaces Beatrice in the Empyrean. He explains the order of the heavenly rose and prays to Mary that Dante may see God.

characters.name: Francesca da Rimini
characters.text: Daughter of Guido da Polenta of Ravenna, married to Gianciotto Malatesta and killed by him with his brother Paolo, her lover, around 1285. In Inferno 5 she tells the story of their love in the language of courtly poetry, and her speech has been read both as a cry of tragic passion and as a self-deceiving justification.

characters.name: Farinata degli Uberti
characters.text: A Ghibelline leader who defeated the Florentine Guelfs at Montaperti in 1260 but opposed the destruction of Florence; he was condemned posthumously as a heretic. In Inferno 10 he rises from his burning tomb, proud and scornful, and predicts the difficulty of Dante's return from exile.

characters.name: Pier della Vigna
characters.text: Chancellor and poet at the court of the Emperor Frederick II, accused of treachery, blinded and imprisoned, who killed himself in 1249. In Inferno 13 he speaks from a tree in the wood of the suicides and protests his loyalty to his lord.

characters.name: Brunetto Latini
characters.text: Florentine notary, statesman and scholar (c. 1220–1294), author of the French encyclopedia Li Livres dou Trésor. Dante treats him with filial love in Inferno 15, though he finds him among the sodomites.

characters.name: Ulysses
characters.text: The Greek hero, punished in a twin flame with Diomedes among the fraudulent counsellors. Dante makes him tell of a last voyage beyond the Pillars of Hercules in pursuit of knowledge, which ends in shipwreck within sight of the mountain of Purgatory.

characters.name: Guido da Montefeltro
characters.text: A Ghibelline commander who became a Franciscan friar and gave fraudulent counsel to Boniface VIII after the pope absolved him in advance. In Inferno 27 his false trust in absolution is set against his son Buonconte's last-minute repentance in Purgatorio 5.

characters.name: Count Ugolino
characters.text: Ugolino della Gherardesca, a Pisan noble accused of treachery, imprisoned with his sons and grandsons by Archbishop Ruggieri and starved to death in 1289. In Inferno 33 he gnaws Ruggieri's skull in the ice and tells the story of their deaths.

characters.name: Lucifer
characters.text: Also called Dis, the rebel angel fallen from heaven, frozen to the waist at the centre of the earth. He has three faces and six wings, chews Judas, Brutus and Cassius, and weeps; he is the poem's image of evil as absolute loss.

characters.name: Cato of Utica
characters.text: The Roman Stoic who killed himself in 46 BC rather than submit to Julius Caesar. Dante makes this pagan suicide the guardian of the mountain of Purgatory, and implies he will be saved, an example of his reverence for Roman virtue and liberty.

characters.name: Manfred
characters.text: King of Sicily, illegitimate son of Frederick II, excommunicated and killed at Benevento in 1266. In Purgatorio 3 he tells how his repentance at death saved him despite the curses of the Church.

characters.name: Sordello
characters.text: A thirteenth-century troubadour from the region of Mantua who wrote in Provençal. His embrace of his fellow Mantuan Virgil provokes Dante's invective against Italy, and he guides the poets to the valley of the princes.

characters.name: Statius
characters.text: The Roman poet of the Thebaid (c. AD 45–96), whom Dante makes a secret convert to Christianity through the reading of Virgil. Freed from Purgatory in Canto 21, he accompanies Dante and Virgil to the summit and is a living proof of what poetry can do.

characters.name: Matelda
characters.text: The lady who sings and gathers flowers in the Earthly Paradise, explains its nature and draws Dante through Lethe and Eunoe. She is not named until Purgatorio 33, and her identity and meaning are much debated.

characters.name: Piccarda Donati
characters.text: Sister of Forese and of the Black leader Corso Donati, taken from her convent and forced to marry. In the sphere of the Moon she explains that the blessed are content with their place, because God's will is their peace.

characters.name: Justinian
characters.text: The sixth-century Roman emperor who codified Roman law. He speaks all of Paradiso 6, telling the providential history of the Roman eagle.

characters.name: Thomas Aquinas
characters.text: The Dominican theologian (c. 1225–1274), whose synthesis of Aristotle and Christian doctrine underlies much of the poem. In the sphere of the Sun he introduces the wise and tells the life of St Francis.

characters.name: Cacciaguida
characters.text: Dante's great-great-grandfather, a crusader who died in the Holy Land around 1147. In the sphere of Mars he describes the sober Florence of his time and prophesies Dante's exile, commissioning him to write the poem.

characters.name: Ripheus and Trajan
characters.text: A Trojan hero whom Virgil called the most just of men, and the Roman emperor whose justice to a widow became a legend. Both appear in the eye of the eagle of Jupiter as pagans saved by grace, a surprise that the poem makes deliberate.

characters.name: Boniface VIII
characters.text: Pope from 1294 to 1303, whose interference in Florence led to Dante's exile. He is still alive in 1300 and therefore cannot appear in Hell, but his damnation is predicted in Inferno 19, and he is condemned by St Peter in Paradiso 27.

characters.name: Henry VII
characters.text: Henry of Luxembourg, Holy Roman Emperor, who came to Italy in 1310 to restore imperial order and died in 1313. Dante supported him with letters, and Beatrice shows him his seat in the Empyrean in Paradiso 30.

themes.title: Love and its ordering
text: The poem is built on a single idea of love. Love moves the universe, it moves the creature towards its end, and when it is misdirected it is the root of every sin. Virgil's discourses at the centre of the Purgatorio explain how love can be turned to evil, too weak for the good, or excessive towards lesser goods, and the whole structure of the mountain follows [[singleton1958]].

The journey therefore is a re-education of desire. Francesca's love that does not let the beloved go, Dante's love for Beatrice and the final love that moves the sun belong to one continuum, and the poem asks how the first can become the last.

themes.title: Divine justice
text: The gate of Hell declares that it was made by justice and love together, and the damned suffer punishments that express their sins. The poem asks the reader to accept a justice that is often painful to contemplate, and the pilgrim's pity is repeatedly tested.

Yet the poem does not hide the questions that justice raises. The fate of the virtuous pagans, the man born on the Indus, the damned Virgil and the saved Ripheus are confronted openly, and the answer, that divine justice exceeds human understanding, does not silence the pathos of the problem [[foster1977]] [[barolini1984]].

themes.title: Free will
text: Against astrological and deterministic theories, the poem insists that human beings are free and therefore responsible for their actions. Marco Lombardo's discourse in Purgatorio 16 and Beatrice's teaching on vows put free will at the heart of the moral universe.

The poem's whole system of rewards and punishments depends on this freedom, and its hope for the world also depends on it: if the world has gone astray, the cause is in humans, and humans can change [[boyde1981]].

themes.title: Church and Empire
text: Dante believed that God had given mankind two guides, the pope for eternal life and the emperor for temporal life, and that the confusion of the two was the cause of the world's corruption. The poem attacks the greed and worldly ambition of popes, from Nicholas III in Hell to Peter's invective in Paradiso 27, and celebrates the providential role of the Roman Empire.

Joan Ferrante showed how deeply this political vision shapes the whole poem: Hell is the image of corrupt society, Purgatory of a society being reformed, and Paradise of the perfect community [[ferrante1984]] [[shaw1996]].

themes.title: Exile and Florence
text: Florence is everywhere in the poem, as a city of envy, avarice and factional violence, and as a lost home. The prophecies of exile build to the clear statement in Paradiso 17, and in Paradiso 25 the poet still hopes to return.
The exile's perspective gives the poem its sharpness and its universality. Dante writes as a man with no city, whose only citizenship is in the heavenly community and in the poem itself [[took2020]].

themes.title: Poetry and its authority
text: The poem is full of poets, from the classical poets of Limbo to Statius, Guinizzelli and Arnaut, and of reflections on the poet's own work. Dante measures himself against Virgil, Ovid and Lucan, and tells his own history of the Italian lyric.

Above all, the poem claims to be true, a vision granted by God and a sacred poem 'to which both heaven and earth have set their hand'. Barolini has argued that the poem's techniques of narrative, its encounters and its claims of truth deserve attention in their own right [[barolini1984]] [[barolini1992]].

themes.title: Language and the ineffable
text: The poem moves from the harsh rhymes of the lower Inferno to the images of the Paradiso, where the poet repeatedly confesses that memory and speech fail him. Language itself becomes a theme in Nimrod's babble, in Adam's account of the first speech and in the coinage of new words such as trasumanar.

The admissions of failure are part of the poem's art: the poet uses them to suggest experiences that no language can contain, and to mark the point at which human speech gives way to vision [[jacoff2007]].

themes.title: Conversion and the self
text: The journey is a conversion, from the dark wood to the vision of God, and it follows patterns of conversion from Scripture and Augustine. The confession in the Earthly Paradise turns that pattern into a personal story of sin and repentance.

Freccero argued that the poem itself is the product of this conversion: the poet can write because he has died to his old self, and the distance between pilgrim and poet is the distance between the old self and the new [[freccero1986]].

motifs.title: Numbers and the Trinity
motifs.text: The poem's form reflects the Trinity: three cantiche of thirty-three cantos, a total of one hundred (the perfect number ten squared), and the three-line tercets of terza rima. Each realm is divided into nine or ten parts, and the number three and its multiples appear throughout, from the three beasts to the three faces of Lucifer and the three circles of the final vision. Singleton made the poem's symmetries a key to its meaning [[singleton1954]].

motifs.title: Contrapasso
motifs.text: The principle that punishment fits the sin, stated by Bertran de Born in Inferno 28. The punishments are often images of the sin itself, so that the damned are shown to have chosen what they suffer. Purgatory has a corresponding but healing logic, with each penance remedying the vice [[durling1996]].

motifs.title: Light
motifs.text: The Inferno is dark, the Purgatorio passes through days and nights, and the Paradiso is made of light. The blessed appear as lights, God as a point and a flash, and the Empyrean as 'pure light'. Dante's theology of light draws on medieval optics and on the Neoplatonic idea that light is the first form of creation [[boyde1981]].

motifs.title: The stars ending each cantica
motifs.text: Each of the three cantiche ends on the word stelle, 'stars': Dante comes out of Hell to see the stars again, leaves the Earthly Paradise ready to rise to them, and ends moved by the love that moves them. The repetition binds the three parts of the journey and points its direction upwards [[singleton1954]].

motifs.title: Prophecies of exile
motifs.text: Ciacco, Farinata, Brunetto, Vanni Fucci, Currado Malaspina, Oderisi and others predict, more or less darkly, the misfortunes of Dante and his party, until Cacciaguida tells the whole story in Paradiso 17. The device allows events after 1300 to be included in a poem set in that year, and it makes Dante's exile a thread running through the whole journey [[took2020]].

motifs.title: Journeys and voyages
motifs.text: The poem uses images of the road and the sea: the pilgrim's lost way, Ulysses' voyage, the boat of souls at Purgatory, the poet's little vessel and the warning to readers in small boats. Ulysses' 'mad flight' recurs as an image of the danger of a journey without grace [[boitani1994]] [[freccero1986]].

symbols.title: The three beasts
symbols.text: The leopard (Longfellow's 'panther'), the lion and the she-wolf block Dante's ascent in Inferno 1. The early commentators read them as lust, pride and avarice, others as the three kinds of sin in Hell or as political powers such as Florence, France and the papacy [[sayers1949]] [[durling1996]]. The she-wolf, the worst, is linked with the greed that the poem condemns everywhere.

symbols.title: The dark wood
symbols.text: The selva oscura of the opening line is the state of sin and confusion in which the journey begins. It is answered at the summit of Purgatory by the 'divine forest' of the Earthly Paradise, the wood restored to its first innocence.

symbols.title: Lucifer
symbols.text: The once-beautiful angel at the bottom of the universe, frozen, silent and weeping, with three faces that parody the Trinity. He is the point farthest from God, the source of cold rather than fire, and his body is the ladder by which the pilgrim leaves Hell.

symbols.title: The mountain
symbols.text: Purgatory is a mountain rising from the sea in the southern hemisphere, formed, Dante says, by the earth that fled from Lucifer's fall. It is the hill of Inferno 1 that Dante could not climb alone, and the mountain that Ulysses saw before his shipwreck; its ascent becomes easier as the soul is purified.

symbols.title: The rose
symbols.text: The white rose of the Empyrean, in whose petals the blessed sit, gathers the whole community of the saved into one image. The rose was a traditional symbol of Mary and of love, and Dante makes it the final figure of the city of God.

debates.title: Allegory and the Letter to Cangrande
text: The Letter to Can Grande della Scala, which dedicates the Paradiso to the lord of Verona, explains the poem as 'polysemous', with a literal sense and an allegorical sense, and illustrates the four senses of scripture with the psalm of the Exodus. Charles Singleton argued that the Comedy uses the 'allegory of the theologians', in which the literal sense is historically true, rather than the 'allegory of the poets', in which a fiction hides a truth; his phrase that the fiction of the poem is that it is not fiction became famous. Robert Hollander developed the argument in his Allegory in Dante's Commedia [[singleton1954]] [[hollander1969]].

The letter's authenticity is itself disputed. Some scholars have argued that its opening dedication may be Dante's but its literary theory is a later compilation; Henry Ansgar Kelly argued against Dante's authorship, while Hollander defended it in a book-length study. The question matters because the letter has been the main external evidence for reading the poem allegorically [[kelly1989]] [[hollander1993]].

debates.title: Auerbach and figura
text: Erich Auerbach argued that Dante's poem depends on figural interpretation, in which a historical event or person is both real in itself and a prefiguration of a future fulfilment, as the Old Testament prefigures the New. In the afterlife the souls appear as the fulfilment of their earthly lives: Cato, Virgil and Beatrice are historical persons and also figures of a truth beyond them [[auerbach1959]] [[auerbach1961]].

Auerbach's essay on Farinata and Cavalcante in Mimesis showed how the figural view makes possible the intense realism of the encounters: eternity does not cancel character but intensifies it. Giuseppe Mazzotta later extended this approach to the poem's understanding of history [[auerbach1953]] [[mazzotta1979]].

debates.title: Francesca: sympathy and judgement
text: For Romantic readers Francesca was a tragic heroine, and Dante's faint was a sign of the poet's own sympathy against the harshness of his theology. Twentieth-century critics, often following the moral readings of commentators, emphasised her self-deception, her blaming of love and the book, and her use of the language of the love poetry that Dante himself had written.

More recent scholarship has looked at the historical case, the gendering of the episode and its place in the poem's structure. Barolini argued that the canto deliberately sets romance against a historical crime and shows Dante's art of creating sympathy for a judged soul [[barolini2000]] [[kirkpatrick1987]].

debates.title: Ulysses' last voyage
text: Dante's Ulysses is a figure of heroic curiosity and of a fatal transgression. Romantic and humanist readers admired his speech as an expression of the dignity of the human search for knowledge, and later writers from Tennyson to Primo Levi adopted it.

Others read the voyage as the 'mad flight' of an intellect without grace, and as the opposite of Dante's own journey, which reaches the mountain by humility. Freccero, Boitani and others have shown how the poem returns to the image of Ulysses' ship, so that the episode is part of the poem's reflection on its own daring [[freccero1986]] [[boitani1994]].

debates.title: Virgil and the salvation of pagans
text: Virgil, the guide who brings Dante to Beatrice, is damned to Limbo, and the poem never hides the sadness of his fate. At the same time Cato, Statius, Trajan and Ripheus are saved, and the eagle in Paradiso 19 admits that the question of the virtuous unbelievers is a mystery.

Kenelm Foster saw a tension between Dante's humanist admiration for the ancient world and his Augustinian theology. Barolini has stressed that Dante's treatment of Virgil is a deliberate construction in which the poem's love for its master is never allowed to escape the truth of his loss [[foster1977]] [[barolini1984]].

debates.title: Dante's politics and the Monarchia
text: The poem's attacks on the papacy and on Florence and its praise of the Roman Empire are rooted in Dante's political theory. In the Monarchia he argued that a universal monarch was necessary for human peace and that the emperor's authority came directly from God. The treatise was burned as heretical in 1329 and put on the Index of prohibited books in the sixteenth century [[shaw1996]].

Joan Ferrante argued that the whole poem is shaped by a political vision of human society, in which the sins of Hell are social sins and Paradise is a perfect community. The dating of the Monarchia, before or during the writing of the Paradiso, remains debated [[ferrante1984]].

debates.title: The 'undivine' Comedy
text: Teodolinda Barolini argued in The Undivine Comedy that critics too often accept the poem's own claims to truth and read it as a theological document. She proposed 'detheologizing' the reading, paying attention to the narrative techniques by which the poem creates the illusion of a true vision.

The approach has been widely influential, but some scholars argue that it underestimates the theological conviction behind the poem. The debate concerns how far a modern reader should accept the poem's own claims to be inspired [[barolini1992]] [[jacoff2007]].

debates.title: Beatrice
text: Who is Beatrice? Boccaccio identified her with Beatrice Portinari, and most scholars accept the identification, but her role in the poem goes far beyond biography. She has been read as theology, as divine wisdom, as grace and as a figure of Christ.

Singleton argued that her coming in the Earthly Paradise is modelled on the coming of Christ, and Auerbach saw her as a figura in which the real woman is fulfilled. Recent critics have also studied how the poem makes a woman the bearer of authority, and how Dante's devotion to her combines personal love and theology [[singleton1958]] [[auerbach1961]] [[jacoff2007]].

quotes.quote:
Midway upon the journey of our life
I found myself within a forest dark,
For the straightforward pathway had been lost.
quotes.explanation: The opening, 'Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita', sets the journey in the middle of a human life and makes Dante's crisis representative. The dark wood and the lost way begin the poem's allegory of sin and conversion.

quotes.who: The inscription on the gate of Hell
quotes.explanation: The gate speaks in the first person, insisting on the eternity of Hell; a few lines later it ends with 'Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate'. The inscription also says that Hell was made by divine power, wisdom and love.

quotes.quote:
And she to me: “There is no greater sorrow
Than to be mindful of the happy time
In misery, and that thy Teacher knows.
quotes.explanation: Francesca's lament before she tells of the book is one of the most quoted passages in the poem. Its sadness and its literary allusion to Boethius make her both a tragic figure and a self-conscious speaker.
Ulysses' exhortation to his crew, which urges them to pursue virtue and knowledge, has been read as a noble expression of human dignity and as the rhetoric of a fraudulent counsellor.
The excommunicated king tells how he was saved by a last repentance. The poem stresses the width of God's mercy against the narrowness of human judgement.
Dante's words to the vanished Virgil translate Dido's line in Aeneid 4. At the moment of meeting Beatrice he speaks in Virgil's words, and the farewell to his guide follows.

quotes.quote:
And his will is our peace; this is the sea
To which is moving onward whatsoever
It doth create, and all that nature makes.
quotes.explanation: 'E 'n la sua volontade è nostra pace': the souls in the lowest heaven are perfectly happy because their will is one with God's. The line expresses the cantica's whole idea of blessedness.

quotes.quote:
Thou shalt have proof how savoureth of salt
The bread of others, and how hard a road
The going down and up another’s stairs.
quotes.explanation: The prophecy of exile: Dante will learn how salty the bread of others tastes and how hard it is to climb another's stairs. Personal suffering is placed at the centre of the heavenly journey.

quotes.quote:
Thou Virgin Mother, daughter of thy Son,
Humble and high beyond all other creature,
The limit fixed of the eternal counsel,
quotes.explanation: 'Vergine Madre, figlia del tuo figlio': Bernard's prayer to the Virgin is built on paradox, and it prepares for the final vision.

quotes.quote: The Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
quotes.explanation: The final line, 'l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle': after the poet's imagination fails, his will and desire are moved like a wheel by divine love. The poem ends with the word stelle, like the other two cantiche.

questions.q: Why does Dante choose Virgil as his guide, and what does Virgil's fate in the poem suggest about classical culture?
questions.hint: Think about Inferno 1 and 4, Statius in Purgatorio 21–22, and Virgil's disappearance in Purgatorio 30.

questions.q: How far does the poem invite the reader to share Dante's pity for Francesca?
questions.hint: Consider the language of her speech, the role of the book, the pilgrim's faint and the place of the canto in the structure of Hell.

questions.q: What is the contrapasso, and how well does it explain the punishments of Hell?
questions.hint: Start from Inferno 28.142 and test the principle on the gluttons, the simonists, the soothsayers and the traitors in the ice.

questions.q: Is Ulysses a hero or a warning?
questions.hint: Compare his speech with the pilgrim's journey, with Purgatorio 1 and with the siren of Purgatorio 19.

questions.q: How does Purgatory differ from Hell in its treatment of time, community and pain?
questions.hint: Look at the prayers, songs and examples on the terraces, the earthquake for Statius and the souls' wish to be remembered.

questions.q: What is the relation between love and sin in the Comedy?
questions.hint: Read Virgil's discourses in Purgatorio 17 and 18 and compare Francesca, Cunizza and the final line of the poem.

questions.q: How does Dante combine personal autobiography with universal vision?
questions.hint: Consider the prophecies of exile, the confession to Beatrice and the opening of Paradiso 25.

questions.q: What is Beatrice: a remembered woman, an allegory, or both?
questions.hint: Compare the Vita Nuova with Purgatorio 30–31 and with Beatrice's teaching role in the Paradiso; think about Auerbach's idea of figura.

questions.q: How does the Paradiso represent what it says cannot be represented?
questions.hint: Look at the ineffability topos, the doctrine of accommodation in Paradiso 4 and the image of the geometer in Paradiso 33.

questions.q: What does the poem say about the relation between Church and Empire?
questions.hint: Compare Marco Lombardo in Purgatorio 16, Justinian in Paradiso 6, Peter's invective in Paradiso 27 and the Monarchia.
